catalog_quote: SP has three degrees of stress, which are assigned from right to left. Primary stress may fall on the penultimate or ultimate syllable, depending on syllable weight. Secondary stress is assigned to the leftmost syllable, not including clitics. Tertiary stress falls on the heaviest syllable (i.e. containing a long vowel or a closed syllable) preceding primary stress. Clitics are extrametrical and do not bear stress. [p. 88] ... Primary stress in SP falls on the penultimate syllable, as shown in (2.136). ... There are four exceptions to this rule. These exceptions include: heavy final syllables (CVVC[+nasal]) the allomorphic alternations of the completive (and incompletive in one context), words borrowed from Spanish, and vocatives. new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (1049 pp., native text layer) at PDF p. 131 (printed p. 88) and PDF p. 137 (printed p. 94), both via extracted text and rendered page images. The p. 88 passage is present exactly as quoted ("SP has three degrees of stress, which are assigned from right to left. Primary stress may fall on the penultimate or ultimate syllable, depending on syllable weight. Secondary stress is assigned to the leftmost syllable, not including clitics. Tertiary stress falls on the heaviest syllable (i.e. containing a long vowel or a closed syllable) preceding primary stress. Clitics are extrametrical and do not bear stress."); the only difference is a footnote marker superscript 20 after "Clitics" and the…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress is penultimate by default within the stressable word (clitics excluded); a heavy final syllable (long vowel + consonant, or one made heavy by the completive suffix) attracts stress to the ultima; Spanish loans and vocatives also take final stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress on the leftmost syllable of the stressable word after clitics (p. 97); tertiary stress on the heaviest syllable between secondary and primary stress, leftmost if equal weight, with acknowledged exceptions and 'no definitive experiments' (p. 98).
new_statements.exceptions: Four exceptions to penultimate stress (pp. 94-97): (i) heavy final syllables CVVC[+nasal], e.g. /kaːma=hoːm/ [kaːmˈhoːm] 'in the field', /wisteːn/ [wisˈteːn] 'two'; (ii) allomorphy of the completive suffix /-W/ (posited /-wi/) making the final syllable heavy, and the incompletive /-pa/ after passive /-taH/ in one context; (iii) Spanish loans preserving source stress (kapéel 'coffee', rabríl 'April', galán); (iv) vocatives, mostly kinship terms, take final stress (/piːʃiɲ/ [piˈʃiɲ] 'Man!', [ʧomˈoʔ] 'Grandma!'). Foster & Foster 1948 (p. 9) instead describe a word-class split: nouns, stative verbs, attributives, pronouns, numerals penultimate loud stress; active verbs final loud stress; stress inherent in some suffixes (-hom loud, -pa weak) and shifting under suffixation and compounding.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the 'stressable word' = stem plus affixes, with proclitics and enclitics extrametrical (§2.4.1, pp. 88-93); examples are phonemic/phonetic citation forms of single words and clitic+word groups; assignment described as right-to-left and weight-sensitive (heavy = long vowel or closed syllable).
new_statements.identity_note: The source describes Sierra Popoluca / Soteapanec (native name Nuntajɨɨyi) as spoken in Soteapan, Veracruz, i.e. the language Glottolog high1276 (ISO poi); no separate dialect is singled out. Foster & Foster 1948 (also Soteapan area) give an older, partly different word-class-based analysis (nouns penultimate, active verbs final), which Boudreault reanalyses as weight-driven via the completive suffix.

sources.note: §2.4 Stress pp. 88-101: three degrees of stress assigned right to left; primary stress on the penultimate syllable, or on a heavy (CVVC[+nasal]) final syllable; four listed exceptions (heavy final syllables, completive/incompletive allomorphy, Spanish loans, vocatives); secondary stress on the leftmost syllable after clitics; tertiary on the heaviest syllable between them; clitics extrametrical.

sources.note: §1.4 Stress p. 3: three levels (loud, medial, weak); loud/weak stress inherent in morphemes, noun and verb stems inherently loud-stressed, stress shifts under suffixation/compounding. §4.22 Stress patterns and shifts pp. 9-10: 'Nouns, stative verbs, attributives, pronouns, and enumeratives of more than one syllable, with certain exceptions, have a loud stress on the penultimate syllable, while active verbs have a loud stress on the final syllable.'
